title: How do you practise cases with a partner and give useful feedback?
description: How to run a practice case for a friend, what good feedback sounds like, and how to get the most out of practising together.
hook: To practise with a partner, have one person run a case from an interviewer script while the other solves it out loud, then give feedback that names one strength, one specific fix with the reason, and one task for the week, before swapping roles. Partner practice adds what solo work cannot: someone watching, interrupting and holding back data until you ask. This guide covers how to run the session, what useful feedback sounds like, and the mistakes that waste practice time.
body:
In this guide

  • Why partner practice matters
  • How to set up a session
  • When you are the interviewer
  • A sample session, with data
  • Giving feedback that helps
  • When you are the candidate
  • Mistakes that waste partner sessions
  • Check yourself

Why partner practice matters

Solo practice builds the skills: structuring, maths, chart reading. A partner tests whether those skills hold up when someone is watching, asks "why?" in the middle of your calculation, or gives you data you did not expect. It also trains the parts of a case that only exist in conversation: asking for information, reading an interviewer's hints and recovering from a wrong turn. Once you can complete a case alone, try to do at least one partner case a week, and more in the final fortnight.

Your partner does not need to know anything about business. Every case in the PrepForCase casebook has an interviewer script that says what to read out, what to reveal and when, and what a good answer looks like. Interviewer mode shows a friend exactly how to run one.

How to set up a session

A good session takes about 90 minutes for two people:

  1. Case one (30 minutes): A interviews, B solves.
  2. Feedback (10 minutes): B self-assesses first, then A gives feedback.
  3. Break (5 minutes).
  4. Case two (30 minutes): swap roles, with a different case type.
  5. Feedback (10 minutes).
  6. Fixes (5 minutes): each person writes down one thing to change next time.

Choose cases the candidate has not seen. Vary the industry and case type between sessions so you do not end up rehearsing a favourite. A video call works as well as a room, as long as the candidate uses paper and the interviewer keeps their camera on.

When you are the interviewer

  • Read the prompt, then stop. Let the candidate recap and ask questions. Do not explain the case further unless asked.
  • Hold back the data. Only share an exhibit when the candidate asks for something like it, or when the script says to. Whether they ask for the right data is part of what you are testing.
  • Stay neutral. No nodding at right answers or frowning at wrong ones. Real interviewers often give little away.
  • Push gently. Ask "why?" once or twice, and "what does that mean for the client?" after a calculation.
  • Do not rescue too early. Let a silence run for ten seconds before you help.
  • Keep time. Most cases should take 25 to 35 minutes. Note the time when the structure is finished and when the recommendation starts.
  • Take notes on evidence: what the candidate said, word for word where you can, at each stage.

A sample session, with data

Say you are running a restaurant profit case. You read: "Our client, a neighbourhood restaurant, has seen profit fall from $400k to $250k in a year, while sales held at about $2M. Why, and what should they do?"

A strong candidate recaps, checks the goal and splits profit into revenue and costs. Because revenue is flat, they ask for the cost breakdown. Only now do you reveal the exhibit: delivery orders rose from 10% to 30% of sales, and the delivery app takes 30% commission. Other costs rose $30k.

The candidate should calculate: commission was 10% × $2M × 30% = $60k and is now 30% × $2M × 30% = $180k, an increase of $120k. Add the $30k of other costs and the $150k fall is fully explained, with delivery commission responsible for 80% of it. A strong close recommends shifting regulars to direct ordering or pickup, and puts a number on the saving.

As the interviewer, your notes might read: "Recap good. Asked for costs at 6 minutes. Calculated commission correctly but did not say it was 80% of the drop until prompted. Recommendation had no saving estimate."

Giving feedback that helps

Start by asking the candidate how they think it went. People notice more than you expect, and it tells you whether they can judge their own performance. Then give feedback in this shape:

  • One strength, so they repeat it.
  • One specific fix, with the reason. Pick the change that would have made the biggest difference.
  • One practice task for the week.

Use the six scored skills as your checklist: recap and questions, structure, maths and charts, driving the case, recommendation and communication. Rate each as ready, improving or needs work, but only talk about one or two.

Weak: "That was pretty good. Maybe be a bit more structured and commercial."
Strong: "Your recap was clear and your maths was right first time. To improve: you found that delivery commission rose $120k but never said it was 80% of the drop, so I had to prompt you. Next time, say what each number means before moving on. This week: after every calculation in your practice, finish the sentence 'this matters because'."

Evidence beats impressions. "You correctly found the commission increase, but your recommendation did not estimate the saving" can be acted on; "be more commercial" cannot.

When you are the candidate

  • Treat it like the real thing: use paper, speak out loud and keep to time.
  • Ask for honest feedback, and write down the one fix.
  • Do not argue with feedback in the moment. Ask questions to understand it.
  • Take your turn as interviewer seriously. Hearing someone else struggle with a vague structure teaches you to recognise your own.

Mistakes that waste partner sessions

  • Reading out all the data at once. The candidate never has to ask for anything, so a key skill goes untested.
  • Feedback that is only praise. Being kind is good. Being vague is not.
  • Ten pieces of feedback. Nobody can fix ten things at once. Choose one or two.
  • Repeating the same case. Once you know the answer, you are rehearsing, not practising.
  • Chatting instead of casing. Agree the timings at the start and stick to them.

Check yourself

1. Your candidate goes quiet for 20 seconds after you share an exhibit. What do you do?

Show the answer

After about ten seconds, prompt lightly: "Talk me through what you're looking at." Do not point to the answer. Note the silence in your feedback.

2. Rewrite this feedback to make it useful: "Your maths was a bit messy."

Show the answer

"In the commission calculation you multiplied before converting 30% to a decimal and lost a zero. Next time, write the formula and units down first, then say each step out loud."

3. In the sample case, what if delivery had risen from 10% to 20% of sales instead?

Show the answer

Commission would be 20% × $2M × 30% = $120k, up $60k from $60k. With the $30k of other costs, that explains $90k of a $150k fall, so the candidate should look for another $60k elsewhere.

Where to go next

If you do not have a partner yet, build your foundations with practising on your own. Pick your next case from the casebook, and use what to say at each stage as a checklist when you give feedback.
